lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 34-year-old woman is back for her fourth admission this year with melaena and a haemoglobin of 62 g/L. Each time she has had an upper endoscopy ("normal") and a colonoscopy ("normal"), been transfused, and gone home on iron. She has now received 22 units of blood in eighteen months. Somewhere between her stomach and her caecum — in the 6 metres of small bowel that neither scope reached — something is bleeding, and everyone has stopped looking. Tonight we go into the mid-gut.

1 · 🗺️ Definitions — say the right words

The vocabulary here is a minefield, and getting it wrong sends patients down the wrong pathway. The 2015 ACG guideline formally retired the term "obscure GI bleeding" as a first-line label and renamed the territory small-bowel bleeding, reserving "obscure" for bleeding that persists after a negative capsule study. Learn the map:

TermMeaning
Overt bleedingVisible blood — melaena, haematochezia, or haematemesis. The patient or the nurse sees it.
Occult bleedingNo visible blood: iron-deficiency anaemia and/or a positive faecal occult blood / FIT test, found on screening.
Small-bowel bleedingBleeding from a source between the ampulla/ligament of Treitz and the ileocaecal valve — the "mid-GI tract" that standard OGD and colonoscopy cannot reach.
Obscure GI bleeding (OGIB)Bleeding of unknown origin that persists or recurs after a negative bidirectional endoscopy AND a negative small-bowel evaluation (e.g. capsule). The true "we still don't know" category.
Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy together see the two ends of a long tube. Between the ligament of Treitz and the ileocaecal valve lies the mid-gut — and that is where the "normal scopes" are hiding the answer.
💡 Why the scopes miss it

A standard gastroscope reaches the second part of the duodenum (occasionally the third); a colonoscope reaches the caecum and sometimes intubates the terminal ileum for a few centimetres. That still leaves roughly 4–6 metres of jejunum and ileum unvisualised. "Normal OGD and colonoscopy" does not mean "no source" — it means "no source in the 20% of the gut we can easily see."

2 · 🔍 First, re-examine the negatives — the missed lesions

Before you send anyone into the small bowel, remember that the commonest cause of "obscure" bleeding is a lesion within reach that was missed the first time. Landmark second-look series find a source in the upper or colonic reach in a meaningful minority. Classic mid-reach missers:

  • Cameron erosions — linear erosions on the neck of a large hiatus hernia, easy to slide past on a quick withdrawal.
  • Dieulafoy lesion — a large-calibre submucosal artery with a pinpoint mucosal defect; bleeds torrentially, then looks like normal mucosa when quiescent.
  • Angiodysplasia (GAVE / gastric antral vascular ectasia) — the "watermelon stomach," easily dismissed as gastritis.
  • Post-bulbar duodenal ulcers and small ampullary lesions beyond a cursory D2 view.
  • Right-colon angioectasia behind folds, or a caecal lesion in a poorly-prepped colon.
⚠️ Before capsule, repeat the obvious

ACG advises a second-look endoscopy — repeat the OGD (with a good look at D2/D3 and the cardia in retroflexion) and consider repeat colonoscopy — before committing to small-bowel work-up, especially if the first studies were done in a bleeding, poorly-prepped, or hurried patient. A push enteroscopy at the second-look can reach the proximal jejunum. Yields on second-look are far from trivial.

3 · 🎂 Causes by age — the pattern that guides you

The single most useful heuristic in small-bowel bleeding is age, because the vascular and neoplastic causes cluster very differently across the lifespan.

Age bandThink first of…
< 40 yearsMeckel's diverticulum, Dieulafoy lesion, small-bowel tumours (GIST, carcinoid, lymphoma), inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's), polyposis syndromes (Peutz–Jeghers).
> 40–60 yearsAngiodysplasia (angioectasia), NSAID enteropathy, tumours, Dieulafoy.
> 60 yearsAngiodysplasia (the single commonest cause in the elderly), NSAID-induced ulcers/diaphragm disease, ischaemia, tumours.
💡 Two memory hooks

Meckel's "rule of 2s": ~2% of the population, ~2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, ~2 inches long, often presents before age 2, and 2 tissue types (gastric and pancreatic ectopia). It bleeds because ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid onto adjacent ileal mucosa. In the young with brisk painless small-bowel bleeding, think Meckel's. In the elderly with recurrent iron-deficiency and vascular comorbidity, think angiodysplasia.

Angiodysplasia / angioectasia deserves special attention: thin-walled, dilated, tortuous submucosal vessels, degenerative and increasingly common with age. Associations that should make you look harder: aortic stenosis and LVADs (Heyde-type acquired von Willebrand from high shear), chronic kidney disease (uraemic platelet dysfunction), and hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. They are frequently multiple, which is why they recur and why a single therapeutic zap is often not curative.

NSAID enteropathy is under-recognised: NSAIDs cause not just gastroduodenal ulcers but small-bowel erosions, ulcers, and pathognomonic "diaphragm disease" — thin concentric fibrotic webs that can bleed and obstruct. Always take a forensic drug history, including over-the-counter ibuprofen and low-dose aspirin.

4 · 🎥 The workup — modality by modality

Once bidirectional endoscopy is genuinely negative and the patient is stable, the small bowel is the target. The tools, in the order the guideline deploys them:

Video capsule endoscopy (VCE) — first-line for stable obscure bleeding

An ingestible camera that photographs the entire small bowel as it passes. ACG makes VCE the first-line small-bowel test in stable overt-obscure and occult small-bowel bleeding — it is non-invasive, images the whole mid-gut, and its findings direct the more invasive next step. Diagnostic yields cluster around 50–65%, and are highest when done closer to the bleeding episode (yield falls the longer you wait).

⚠️ Capsule pitfalls

Its Achilles heels: (1) no therapy and no biopsy — it only looks; (2) it can miss lesions in the duodenum and around the ampulla (rapid transit, blind spots) — a bleeding source there may be better found by repeat endoscopy; (3) capsule retention (~1–2%, higher in Crohn's/NSAID strictures or known obstruction) can precipitate obstruction and rarely need surgery. If stricture risk is high, deploy a dissolvable patency capsule first. Never place a capsule in suspected obstruction.

Device-assisted (deep) enteroscopy — the therapeutic arm

Double-balloon and single-balloon enteroscopy pleat the small bowel over an overtube, allowing deep intubation from above (antegrade, per-oral) or below (retrograde, per-anal). Unlike the capsule, this is where you biopsy, tattoo, and treat — argon plasma coagulation of angioectasia, clip or inject a Dieulafoy, dilate a stricture, resect a polyp. It is usually targeted by the capsule finding (the capsule tells you whether to go from the top or the bottom). Total enteroscopy (seeing the whole small bowel in one or two combined passes) is achievable in experienced hands but not always necessary.

Cross-sectional imaging — CT / MR enterography

CT enterography (neutral oral contrast to distend the lumen + timed IV contrast) is excellent for mass lesions and Crohn's that a capsule can under-call, and is often complementary to VCE. MR enterography avoids radiation — favoured in young patients and in Crohn's who need repeated imaging. For active brisk bleeding, CT angiography can localise extravasation (detects rates ≈ 0.3–0.5 mL/min) and triage to catheter angiography.

Meckel's scan

In a young patient with obscure bleeding, the technetium-99m pertechnetate scan ("Meckel's scan") is targeted at ectopic gastric mucosa, which takes up the tracer. Sensitivity is highest in children (~85–90%) and lower in adults; a negative scan does not exclude Meckel's, and sensitivity can be improved with pentagastrin/H2-blocker pre-treatment. It is cheap, non-invasive, and highly specific when positive.

Emergency localisation of the actively, briskly bleeding patient

  • CT angiography first if unstable-but-resuscitatable — fast, widely available, maps the target for the interventional radiologist.
  • Catheter mesenteric angiography ± embolisation — detects faster bleeds (~0.5–1.0 mL/min) and can treat.
  • Tagged red-cell (⁹⁹mTc-RBC) scan — most sensitive for slow/intermittent bleeding (~0.1–0.2 mL/min) but only regionalises, and is prone to error from pooling/transit; use to decide whether angiography is worthwhile.
  • Intra-operative enteroscopy — the last resort for the exsanguinating, unlocalised patient in theatre.

5 · 📊 Modality → yield at a glance

ModalityBest forApprox. diagnostic yield / detection threshold
Second-look OGD/colonoscopyMissed within-reach lesions (Cameron, Dieulafoy, angioectasia)Source found in a meaningful minority
Video capsule endoscopyFirst-line whole-small-bowel survey (stable)~50–65% (higher done early)
Device-assisted enteroscopyDiagnosis + therapy, capsule-directed~60–75%, with treatment in the same sitting
CT / MR enterographyTumours, Crohn's, strictures~40–55% for mass lesions (complementary to VCE)
CT angiographyActive brisk bleedingDetects ≈ 0.3–0.5 mL/min
Catheter angiography ± embolisationActive bleeding, therapeuticDetects ≈ 0.5–1.0 mL/min
Tagged RBC scanSlow/intermittent, regionalisationDetects ≈ 0.1–0.2 mL/min (localises only)
Meckel's scan (⁹⁹mTc-pertechnetate)Ectopic gastric mucosa in the young~85–90% in children; lower in adults

6 · 🧭 The algorithm — putting it together

  1. Is it small-bowel bleeding? Confirm a genuinely adequate, ideally repeated, negative OGD and colonoscopy. Re-look for the missed lesion first.
  2. Is the patient stable or unstable? Unstable / brisk overt → resuscitate → CT angiography → catheter angiography ± embolisation (or straight to angio/OR if exsanguinating). Stable overt or occult → small-bowel pathway.
  3. Stable pathway: video capsule endoscopy first-line (patency capsule first if stricture risk). In a young patient with painless bleeding, add/consider a Meckel's scan.
  4. Capsule positive → device-assisted enteroscopy via the route the capsule indicates (antegrade for proximal, retrograde for distal) to biopsy and treat. Suspected tumour/Crohn's → CT/MR enterography to characterise and stage.
  5. Capsule negative but bleeding continues (true obscure) → do not stop. Repeat capsule (yield rises on rebleeding), CT/MR enterography, deep enteroscopy anyway, or angiography during an active bleed. Consider a missed proximal lesion — repeat OGD.
  6. Refractory recurrent angioectasia → endoscopic ablation of accessible lesions; medical therapy for diffuse disease (see below).
💡 Timing is yield

Every test in obscure bleeding performs better during or soon after active bleeding. A capsule, angiogram, or RBC scan done two weeks after the melaena stopped is often falsely negative. If a patient is actively bleeding, investigate now, not after the weekend.

7 · 💊 When you can't ablate everything — medical therapy for diffuse angioectasia

Recurrent bleeding from multiple or diffuse small-bowel angioectasia — the frail elderly, the LVAD patient, HHT — is where endoscopy alone fails. Options with evidence:

  • Iron replacement (oral or IV) — the foundation; many patients are managed by keeping up with losses.
  • Somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide) — reduce splanchnic flow and transfusion requirements in refractory angiodysplasia.
  • Thalidomide — anti-angiogenic; reduces rebleeding in trials but limited by teratogenicity and neuropathy.
  • Correct the driver — in Heyde syndrome, aortic valve replacement reverses the acquired von Willebrand defect and often cures the bleeding.
☠️ M&M — the tumour nobody would name

A 41-year-old man had five admissions over two years with iron-deficiency anaemia and intermittent melaena. He had three "normal" gastroscopies, two "normal" colonoscopies, and was labelled with "functional" bleeding and treated as an outpatient with iron. A capsule study had actually been requested once but cancelled when his haemoglobin transiently recovered. On his sixth presentation he arrived shocked; a CT finally showed a 4 cm jejunal GIST with a central ulcer, now with liver metastases. At his first admission the tumour had been small and resectable. Lessons: "recurrent iron-deficiency with normal scopes" is small-bowel bleeding until proven otherwise — it is a mandate to image the mid-gut, not a reason to reassure. A young patient with recurrent bleeding needs a small-bowel tumour actively excluded (capsule + enterography), and a transient haemoglobin bump is not a diagnosis. The scopes were normal because the lesion was never in them.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Learn the words: overt vs occult; small-bowel bleeding = source between the ligament of Treitz and the ileocaecal valve; "obscure" is reserved for bleeding that persists after a negative small-bowel study.
  2. "Normal OGD and colonoscopy" leaves 6 metres unseen — and the commonest "obscure" source is a lesion within reach that was missed. Re-look first.
  3. Age triages cause: young → Meckel's, Dieulafoy, tumours, Crohn's; old → angiodysplasia, NSAID enteropathy, tumours.
  4. Video capsule endoscopy is first-line for the stable patient; it looks but cannot treat, and can be retained — screen for strictures.
  5. Device-assisted (double/single-balloon) enteroscopy is the therapeutic arm, targeted by the capsule.
  6. Match the test to the bleed rate: CTA/angiography for brisk, tagged-RBC scan for slow, Meckel's scan for the young — and do them during active bleeding.
  7. Diffuse angioectasia is a medical problem (iron, somatostatin analogues, thalidomide) — and Heyde's is cured by fixing the valve.

moderatorQs.q: A patient has had two normal gastroscopies and two normal colonoscopies but keeps bleeding. What is your very next step, and why not just repeat the scopes again?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: First I make sure the negatives are genuinely adequate — a second-look OGD with careful D2/D3 and retroflexed cardia views catches missed Cameron erosions, a quiescent Dieulafoy, or GAVE, and these within-reach missers are the single commonest cause of so-called obscure bleeding. If a good bidirectional exam is truly negative, I stop repeating the same two tests and image the 4–6 metres they cannot reach: in a stable patient the first-line small-bowel test is video capsule endoscopy, done as close to the bleeding episode as possible because yield falls the longer you wait. The capsule then directs a device-assisted (double/single-balloon) enteroscopy from the top or bottom for biopsy and therapy. Repeating identical scopes a third time without going into the mid-gut is how tumours get missed for years.

moderatorQs.q: How does the patient's age change what you expect to find in small-bowel bleeding?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Age is the most useful single discriminator. In the young (<40) I think Meckel's diverticulum (ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerating adjacent ileum — the 'rule of 2s'), Dieulafoy lesions, small-bowel tumours (GIST, carcinoid, lymphoma), and Crohn's. In the older patient (>60) the dominant cause is angiodysplasia/angioectasia — degenerative, often multiple, and linked to aortic stenosis, LVADs and CKD — together with NSAID enteropathy (ulcers and diaphragm disease) and tumours. So in a 30-year-old with painless brisk bleeding I add a Meckel's scan, whereas in an 80-year-old with recurrent iron-deficiency I expect diffuse angioectasia that may need medical therapy, not just a single ablation.

moderatorQs.q: What are the real limitations of video capsule endoscopy that you must warn the team about before ordering it?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Three big ones. First, it is diagnostic only — no biopsy, no therapy; a positive capsule commits you to a follow-on device-assisted enteroscopy to actually treat. Second, it has blind spots, particularly around the duodenum and ampulla where transit is fast, so a proximal source can be missed and is sometimes better found by repeating the endoscopy. Third, and most dangerous, is capsule retention (~1–2%, much higher with Crohn's or NSAID strictures), which can precipitate obstruction and occasionally require surgery — so it is contraindicated in suspected obstruction, and where stricture risk is high I deploy a dissolvable patency capsule first. Finally, yield is time-dependent: a capsule done two weeks after the bleeding stopped is often falsely negative.

audienceQs.q: The capsule shows an angioectasia in the mid-jejunum. Do I go antegrade or retrograde with the balloon enteroscope?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Let the capsule's transit timing decide. Note the time the capsule takes from the pylorus (or first duodenal image) to the lesion as a fraction of the total small-bowel transit time to the caecum. If the lesion appears in roughly the proximal ~two-thirds of small-bowel transit, go antegrade (per-oral); if it is in the distal third, go retrograde (per-anal). A mid-jejunal lesion is usually reachable antegrade. Tattoo the site when you treat it so it can be relocated, and remember angioectasiae are often multiple — survey the accessible bowel and ablate all you find with argon plasma coagulation in the same sitting.

audienceQs.q: A 25-year-old with painless melaena and normal scopes — what's the one test I shouldn't forget?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The Meckel's scan — a technetium-99m pertechnetate study that lights up ectopic gastric mucosa, the tissue that secretes acid and ulcerates the adjacent ileum to cause the bleed. In a young patient with painless small-bowel bleeding, Meckel's diverticulum is top of the differential ('rule of 2s': ~2% of people, ~2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, often symptomatic before age 2). Sensitivity is highest in children (~85–90%) and lower in adults, and a negative scan doesn't fully exclude it — but it is cheap, non-invasive and highly specific when positive, so it's the test that's easy to forget and embarrassing to miss.

audienceQs.q: My patient is actively passing a lot of maroon blood and is unstable — capsule or something else?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Not the capsule — that's for the stable patient and takes hours to read. For active, brisk bleeding, resuscitate first, then localise fast with CT angiography, which detects extravasation around 0.3–0.5 mL/min and maps the target. Positive or ongoing → catheter mesenteric angiography with embolisation (detects ~0.5–1.0 mL/min and treats in the same procedure). For slower, intermittent bleeding a tagged red-cell scan is more sensitive (~0.1–0.2 mL/min) but only regionalises. The unlocalised exsanguinating patient goes to theatre for intra-operative enteroscopy. The principle: match the tool to the bleeding rate, and investigate while it is actively bleeding.
